opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people underrate this. Right now, there's a big gap between raw model capability and the economic value businesses actually capture. The current systems are, in a sense, really hobbled. They're like a very smart person who's been given five minutes and no context. You drop them into a chatbot window, they don't know anything about your company, your codebase, your Slack history. They can't go off and work on something for hours. They can't use a computer the way a human employee would. So to get value out of them, a business has to do a ton of integration work: figure out which narrow tasks to carve out, build scaffolding, retrain workflows around them. That's slow and expensive, and it's a big part of why adoption lags capability.

What I expect as models get more powerful, and as we do what I'd call "unhobbling," is that the integration burden shrinks dramatically. The endpoint looks less like a chatbot and more like a drop-in remote worker. You onboard it like a new hire: it reads your docs, sits in your Slack, uses your tools, and can be handed a project that would take a person days or weeks. It goes off, works on it, checks its own work, comes back.

And that's a qualitatively different thing for a business. You don't need to redesign your whole organization around a weird new tool. You just plug it in where you'd otherwise hire someone. Paradoxically, the more capable the system, the *easier* it is to deploy, because it can adapt to your processes rather than you adapting to it. So I think there's a sort of sonic boom effect, where intermediate systems require a lot of schlep to be useful, and then at some point the models get good enough that the schlep mostly disappears and economic value starts flowing much faster.

r001.rationale: The response says businesses must do substantial integration work, including carving out tasks and retraining workflows, to get value from current systems.

r002.rationale: It says adoption lags capability, integration is slow and expensive, and more capable models may make that integration burden shrink—implying businesses may encounter stronger systems before completing the costly work for intermediate ones.

r003.rationale: It describes the endpoint as a “drop-in remote worker” that can be onboarded like a new hire and use company tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I think the key thing is that right now, the way AI gets used in a business is this kind of awkward, piecemeal thing. You've got a model that's good at a bunch of tasks, but you have to break your workflow into little chunks, hand each chunk to the model, check the output, stitch it back together. And that integration work is actually really expensive. It's the bottleneck. Every company has to figure out "okay, where exactly in our process does this thing help, how do we prompt it, how do we catch its mistakes." That's a lot of what I'd call the schlep.

And historically that's been true of general-purpose technologies. Electricity is the classic example. Factories had electricity for decades before productivity really jumped, because you had to completely redesign the factory floor around it rather than just swapping the steam engine for a motor. The gains didn't come from the technology existing, they came from reorganizing everything around it, and that took a generation.

What I think changes with much more capable systems is that the systems themselves can do the reorganizing. If you have something that's roughly like a drop-in remote worker, you don't need to figure out the clever decomposition of your job into model-shaped pieces. You just say, "here's the job, here's the context, go." It onboards itself. It figures out the integration. The adoption cost collapses, because the thing you're adopting is smart enough to adopt itself.

So the way I'd put it is: today's models require the business to be smart about using the AI. Future models require the business to be much less smart, because the AI is smart about being used. And that's why I think the economic gains aren't going to be this slow, decades-long diffusion curve. Once you cross the threshold where the system can handle the messy end-to-end task rather than the tidy sub-task, you go from "interesting productivity tool" to "we can just hire a million of these." And at that point the gains stop being bottlenecked on human organizational change, which is the slowest thing in the world, and start being bottlenecked on compute, which you can actually buy.

r001.rationale: The response says current AI requires breaking workflows into pieces and that realizing gains requires costly integration and reorganizing business processes.

r002.rationale: It contrasts costly current integration with future systems that handle their own integration, and says gains can arrive without a slow, decades-long diffusion curve.

r003.rationale: It describes a more capable system as a “drop-in remote worker” that can take a whole job and figure out its integration.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a counterintuitive possibility here, which is that more capable systems are actually easier to deploy. With a system that can do little bits of a job, you have to build a lot of infrastructure around it. You have to figure out which tasks to give it, how to provide the context, how to check its work, and how to integrate the output into what your employees are doing. Those costs can eat up the productivity gains.

Compare that with a system where you can say, “Here’s a project. Go do it.” It can ask questions, use the tools your company already uses, and deal with problems along the way. That looks much more like hiring a remote employee, which businesses already know how to do.

So you don’t necessarily need every company to reinvent its workflow around the limitations of the model. As the model gets better, it can handle more of the existing workflow itself. And being able to complete a whole task reliably can be much more economically valuable than being able to do half of it, even if that half looks impressive in a demo.

r001.rationale: The response says limited systems require substantial surrounding infrastructure and that companies otherwise need to reinvent workflows around model limitations to capture productivity gains.

r002.rationale: It says more capable systems can reduce the need for workflow reinvention, but does not state or clearly imply that they may arrive before businesses undertake the costly integration work.

r003.rationale: It compares a system that can take a project, ask questions, use company tools, and handle problems to hiring a remote employee, which businesses already know how to do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a counterintuitive possibility here, which is that more powerful systems are actually easier to get economic value out of. With a system that can do only a small part of somebody’s job, you have to build a whole workflow around it. You have to figure out where it fits, connect it to your internal systems, and have somebody check its work. Those integration costs can eat up the benefit.

If the system can take a task from beginning to end, the proposition becomes much simpler. You can say, “Here’s a project. Go do it,” in roughly the way you would delegate to an employee. And a sufficiently capable system can help with the integration itself: learn the company’s processes, write the software it needs, ask questions when it gets stuck.

So I wouldn’t assume that adoption necessarily gets harder as the technology advances. Some of what looks like a bottleneck in organizational adoption today might actually be a bottleneck in capability. Once the systems are reliable enough to handle longer stretches of work, the economics could become much more compelling.

r001.rationale: The response says limited-capability systems require building a workflow around them, connecting internal systems, and checking their work, with integration costs that can eat up the benefit.

r002.rationale: The response suggests capability limits may be the bottleneck and that adoption could become easier as systems improve, but it does not say more powerful AI may arrive before businesses undertake the costly integration work.

r003.rationale: The response says an end-to-end system lets a business delegate a project in roughly the way it would to an employee, making the proposition simpler and enabling the system to help with integration.
